title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LVI
paragraphs: Dorothea's trust in Caleb Garth's knowledge had begun when she heard that he approved of her cottages. It grew rapidly during her stay at Freshitt. Sir James persuaded her to ride over both estates with him and Caleb, who fully shared her admiration. He told his wife that Mrs. Casaubon had an understanding of business most unusual in a woman. Remember that by “business” Caleb never meant dealings in money, but the skillful use of labor.

“Most unusual!” Caleb repeated. “She said something I often thought myself as a boy: ‘Mr. Garth, if I live to be old, I'd like to feel that I had improved a large stretch of land and built plenty of good cottages, because the work is healthy while people are doing it, and once it's finished their lives are better for it.’ Those were her exact words. That's how deeply she understands things.”
“But she's womanly, I hope,” said Mrs. Garth. She half suspected that Mrs. Casaubon might not properly appreciate a woman's subordinate place.

“Oh, you can't imagine!” Caleb said, shaking his head. “You'd love to hear her talk, Susan. Such plain words, and a voice like music. Bless me, it reminds me of passages in the ‘Messiah’—‘and straightway there appeared a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying.’ There's a quality in it that satisfies the ear.”

Caleb loved music. Whenever he could afford it, he attended any oratorio performed within reach. He came home filled with profound reverence for that mighty structure of sound, and would sit thoughtfully staring at the floor, his outstretched hands expressing a great deal that words could not.

Given their mutual understanding, it was natural that Dorothea should ask Mr. Garth to manage the business of the three farms and the many rented properties belonging to Lowick Manor. His expectation of finding enough work for two people was rapidly being fulfilled. As he put it, “Business breeds.” One kind of business beginning to breed at that time was railway construction. A proposed line would cross Lowick parish, where cattle had until then grazed in peace, without anything to astonish them. In this way the early struggles of the railway system entered Caleb Garth's affairs, and determined the course of this story for two people dear to him. Building a railway beneath the sea may have its difficulties; but the seabed is not divided among different landowners who demand compensation for injuries to their feelings as well as their property. In the district containing Middlemarch, railways caused as much excitement as the Reform Bill or the approaching terrors of cholera. Women and landowners had the firmest opinions. Women of all ages thought steam travel presumptuous and dangerous. Their argument against it was that nothing would ever persuade them to enter a railway carriage. Landowners might differ in their reasoning as widely as Mr. Solomon Featherstone differed from Lord Medlicote, but they agreed on one point: whether you sold land to the Enemy of mankind or to a company compelled to buy it, such destructive powers must pay landowners very handsomely for permission to injure the human race.

Slower minds, however, such as those of Mr. Solomon and Mrs. Waule, who both occupied their own land, took a long time to reach this conclusion. Their thoughts stuck at the vivid prospect of cutting the Big Pasture in half and leaving triangular pieces that would be “no good anyhow.” Bridges to connect the severed land, and large payments in compensation, seemed distant and unbelievable.

“Every cow will lose her calf, brother,” said Mrs. Waule in deep gloom, “if the railway crosses the Near Close. And I wouldn't be surprised if the mare did too, if she were in foal. It's a poor state of things if they can dig away a widow's property and the law has nothing to say. Once they start, what's to stop them cutting anywhere they please? Everyone knows _I_ can't fight.”

“Best say nothing, and get somebody to send them off with a flea in their ear when they come snooping and measuring,” Solomon said. “That's what people did near Brassing, as far as I understand. This talk about having to take one particular route is all a sham, if the truth were known. Let them cut through another parish. And I don't believe they'll pay anything to make up for bringing a pack of ruffians to trample your crops. Where does a company keep its pocket?”
“Brother Peter—God forgive him—got money out of a company,” said Mrs. Waule. “But that was for manganese. It wasn't for railways blowing you to pieces on every side.”

“Well, Jane, there's this,” Mr. Solomon concluded, cautiously lowering his voice. “The more obstacles we put in their way, the more they'll pay to be allowed through—if they're coming whether we like it or not.”

Mr. Solomon's reasoning was perhaps less sound than he supposed. His cunning had about as much bearing on the progress of railways as a diplomat's cunning has on a general chill or cold afflicting the solar system. Still, he acted on his views in a thoroughly diplomatic fashion: he encouraged suspicion. His side of Lowick was furthest from the village. The laborers lived either in isolated cottages or in the hamlet of Frick, where a watermill and some quarries formed a small center of slow, heavy-shouldered industry.

No one in Frick knew precisely what railways were, but public opinion opposed them. In that grassy corner, the human mind showed none of its proverbial admiration for the unknown. Instead, people assumed that unfamiliar things were likely to hurt the poor man, and that suspicion was the only sensible response. Even rumors of Reform had inspired no visions of a golden age in Frick. There was no definite promise of free grain to fatten Hiram Ford's pig, or a landlord at the “Weights and Scales” who would brew beer for nothing, or an offer from the three neighboring farmers to raise winter wages. Without any clear benefit of that sort among its promises, Reform sounded like a peddler's boasting, which warned any knowing person to be on guard. Frick's men were not badly fed. They were more disposed to a sturdy, muscular distrust than to fanaticism; less inclined to think that heaven took special care of them than that heaven itself was rather likely to cheat them—a tendency plainly visible in the weather.

Frick's outlook was therefore exactly suited to Mr. Solomon Featherstone's influence. He had a more abundant stock of the same ideas, and his suspicion of heaven and earth was better fed and had more leisure. At the time, Solomon supervised the roads. Riding his slow-paced cob, he often made his rounds through Frick to watch the men quarrying stone. He would stop with a mysterious deliberateness which might have made you imagine he had some reason to stay beyond simply lacking the impulse to move. After watching whatever work was going on for a long time, he would lift his eyes a little and study the horizon. Eventually he shook the bridle, touched the horse with his whip, and persuaded it to proceed slowly. A clock's hour hand was quick compared with Mr. Solomon, who enjoyed knowing that he could afford to take his time. He habitually stopped beside every hedger or ditcher for a cautious conversation full of vague designs. He was especially willing to hear news he had already heard, feeling that his partial disbelief gave him an advantage over any storyteller. One day, though, he himself supplied information in a conversation with Hiram Ford, a wagon driver. He asked whether Hiram had seen fellows with staffs and instruments snooping around. They called themselves railway people, but who knew what they really were or what they intended? At the very least, they claimed they were going to cut Lowick parish to pieces.
“Why, we won't be able to get from one place to another,” Hiram said, thinking of his wagon and horses.

“Not at all,” said Mr. Solomon. “And cutting up fine land like we've got in this parish! Let them go into Tipton, I say. But who knows what's behind it? Trade's the reason they give, but in the long run it's the land and the poor man that'll suffer.”
“London fellows, I reckon,” said Hiram, who had a vague idea of London as a center of hostility toward the countryside.

“Yes, certainly. And in places near Brassing, from what I've heard, people attacked them while they were spying, smashed those peeping instruments they carry, and drove them off. They knew better than to come back.”
“Must have been good fun, I'll bet,” said Hiram, whose opportunities for amusement were severely limited.

“Well, I wouldn't interfere with them myself,” Solomon said. “But some say this country's best days are over. The sign of it is these fellows overrunning it, trampling everywhere and wanting to slice it into railways. All so the big trade can swallow the little, till there's not a team of horses left on the land, nor a whip to crack.”
“I'll crack _my_ whip round their ears before they get that far,” said Hiram, as Mr. Solomon shook his bridle and moved on.

Nettle seeds need no soil preparation. The railways' destruction of the countryside became a subject of conversation not only at the “Weights and Scales,” but also in the hayfield. The gathering of workers there offered chances to talk that were rare in the rest of the farming year.

One morning, shortly after the conversation in which Mary Garth admitted her feelings for Fred Vincy to Mr. Farebrother, business took her father to Yoddrell's farm, toward Frick. He had to measure and value an outlying piece of Lowick Manor land which he expected to sell profitably for Dorothea. It must be admitted that Caleb favored getting the best possible terms out of railway companies. He left his gig at Yoddrell's and walked with his assistant and measuring chain to the land. On the way he met the company's agents, who were adjusting their spirit level. After a brief conversation, he left them, remarking that their work would soon bring them back to him at the spot he was going to measure. It was one of those gray mornings after light rain that become delightful around noon, when the clouds open a little and the earth smells sweet along lanes and hedges.

That smell would have been sweeter to Fred Vincy, riding along the lanes, had he not been troubled by fruitless attempts to decide what to do. On one side his father expected him to enter the Church at once; on the other, Mary threatened to give him up if he did. Meanwhile, the everyday working world showed no eagerness for a young gentleman with no capital and no particular skills. For someone of Fred's temperament, matters were made harder by his father's good humor. Believing his son had stopped resisting, Mr. Vincy had sent him on this pleasant ride to inquire about some greyhounds. Even once Fred decided what to do, he would still have to tell his father. But the decision, which had to come first, was admittedly the harder task. What secular occupation existed for a young man whose friends could not secure him an “appointment,” which was gentlemanly, profitable, and required no specialized knowledge? Riding near Frick in this mood, he slowed down to consider whether he dared go round by Lowick Parsonage to see Mary. He could look over the hedges from field to field. Suddenly a noise caught his attention. Across a field on his left, six or seven men in smocks, carrying hayforks, were advancing threateningly on four railway agents who faced them. Caleb Garth and his assistant were hurrying across to help the threatened party. Fred lost a few moments finding the gate. Before he could gallop up, the smocked men—who had found turning hay less urgent after their midday beer—were driving the men in coats ahead of them with their forks. Caleb's assistant, a boy of seventeen, had picked up the spirit level at Caleb's order, and had been knocked down. He seemed to be lying helpless. The men in coats could run faster, and Fred covered their retreat by riding in front of the pursuers and charging suddenly enough to disrupt the chase. “What do you think you're doing, you damned fools?” he shouted. He rode zigzag after the scattered group, slashing to either side with his whip. “I'll identify every one of you before the magistrate. You've knocked that boy down and killed him, for all I know. You'll all be hanged at the next assizes if you're not careful.” Later, Fred laughed heartily when he remembered his own words.

The laborers had been driven back through the gate into their hayfield, and Fred had reined in his horse, when Hiram Ford decided he was far enough away to issue a safe challenge. Turning back, he shouted a defiance he did not know was Homeric.
“You're a coward, that's what you are. Get off your horse, young master, and I'll fight you. You daren't come without your horse and whip. I'd soon knock the wind out of you, I would.”

“Wait a minute. I'll be back shortly, and I'll fight every one of you in turn if you like,” Fred said, confident of his boxing abilities against these dearly beloved brethren. Just now, though, he wanted to hurry back to Caleb and the fallen boy.
The boy had sprained his ankle and was in considerable pain, but had no other injury. Fred put him on the horse so that he could ride to Yoddrell's and be looked after there.
“Have them stable the horse, and tell the surveyors they can fetch their equipment,” Fred said. “It's safe now.”

“No, no,” said Caleb. “Something's broken here. They'll have to stop for today, and that's probably best. Here, Tom, take these things on the horse in front of you. When they see you coming, they'll turn back.”
“I'm glad I happened along at the right moment, Mr. Garth,” Fred said as Tom rode off. “Who knows what would have happened if the cavalry hadn't arrived in time?”

“Yes, yes, lucky indeed,” said Caleb rather absently. He was looking toward the place where he had been working when they were interrupted. “But—damn it—this is what happens when men behave like fools. My day's work is held up. I can't manage without someone to help with the measuring chain. Still!” Looking annoyed, he began walking toward the spot, apparently forgetting Fred was there. Then he suddenly turned and asked briskly, “What have you got to do today, young fellow?”
“Nothing, Mr. Garth. I'd be delighted to help. Could I?” Fred felt that helping Mary's father would itself be a way of courting her.
“Well, you mustn't object to bending down and getting hot.”
“I don't mind any of that. Only first I want a round with that hulking fellow who challenged me. It would teach him a good lesson. I won't be five minutes.”
“Don't be ridiculous!” said Caleb in his most commanding voice. “I'll speak to the men myself. It's ignorance, all of it. Someone's been feeding them lies. The poor fools don't know any better.”
“Then I'll come along,” Fred said.
“No, no, stay here. I don't need your young hot blood. I can look after myself.”

Caleb was a strong man who scarcely knew fear, except the fear of hurting other people and the fear of making speeches. Now, however, he felt obliged to deliver a small address. Having always worked hard himself, he combined strict ideas about workers with remarkable practical tolerance toward them. He believed that putting in a full day's work, and doing it well, was part of their well-being, as it was the chief source of his own happiness. But he also felt a strong fellowship with them. When he approached, the laborers had not resumed work. They stood in that rural grouping in which each man turns one shoulder toward another, two or three yards away. They looked sulkily at Caleb. He walked quickly, one hand in his pocket and the other tucked between his waistcoat buttons, and stopped among them with his usual mild expression.

“Well, my lads, what's all this?” he began. As usual he spoke in short phrases that seemed full of meaning to him because so many thoughts lay beneath them, like the spreading roots of a plant barely visible above the water. “How did you come to make such a mistake? Somebody's been lying to you. You thought those men over there meant mischief.”
“Aye,” each man answered at a different moment, according to how long it took him to find a reply.

“Nonsense! They mean nothing of the kind. They're finding out where the railway should run. Now, lads, you can't stop the railway. It'll be built whether you like it or not. Fight it and you'll get yourselves into trouble. The law allows those men onto this land. The owner can't object, and if you interfere you'll have the constable and Justice Blakesley to deal with, and handcuffs, and Middlemarch jail. You could be facing all that already, if anyone reported you.”
Caleb paused. Perhaps the finest orator could not have chosen a better moment to pause, or more effective images for this audience.

“But come now, you didn't mean harm. Someone told you the railway was a bad thing. That was a lie. It may do some harm here and there, to this person or that. So does the sun in the sky. But the railway's a good thing.”

“Aye, good for the big folk to make money from,” said old Timothy Cooper. He had stayed behind turning hay while the others went off on their adventure. “I've seen plenty come along since I was young: war and peace, the canals, old King George, the Regent, the new King George, and the new one with a different name. It's all been the same to the poor man. What have canals done for him? They've brought him neither meat nor bacon, nor wages he can save without starving himself to do it. Things have got worse for him since my young days. It'll be the same with railways. They'll only leave the poor man further behind. But anyone who interferes is a fool, and I told these fellows so. This world belongs to the big folk. And you're on their side, Mr. Garth, you are.”

Timothy was a wiry old laborer of a kind still surviving then. He kept his savings in the foot of a stocking, lived in a solitary cottage, and no amount of eloquence could sway him. He had as little feudal loyalty and as little faith as though he had actually read the Age of Reason and the Rights of Man, of which he knew absolutely nothing. Caleb faced a difficulty familiar to anyone who, in unenlightened times and without miraculous assistance, tries to reason with country people who possess an undeniable truth. They have learned it through painful experience, and can drop it like a giant's club on your delicately carved argument for a social benefit they cannot feel. Caleb had no stock of pious platitudes, even if he had wished to use them. His customary way of meeting such difficulties was simply to carry out his “business” faithfully. He answered:

“If you don't think much of me, Tim, never mind. That's not the point just now. Things may be bad for the poor man—they are bad. But I don't want these lads making things worse for themselves. Cattle may be pulling a heavy load, but tipping it into a roadside pit won't help them when some of it is their own feed.”
“We only wanted a bit of fun,” said Hiram, beginning to see the consequences. “That's all we were after.”
“Well then, promise me you won't interfere again, and I'll make sure nobody reports you.”
“I haven't interfered, and I've no need to promise,” Timothy said.
“No, but the others have. Come, I'm working as hard as any of you today, and I haven't much time to spare. Say you'll keep quiet without needing the constable.”
“Aye, we won't interfere. They can do as they please for all we care.” In such words Caleb received their promises, then hurried back to Fred, who had followed him and watched from the gateway.

They began work, and Fred helped energetically. His spirits had lifted. He even thoroughly enjoyed a good slide in the damp earth under the hedge, which dirtied his immaculate summer trousers. Was he elated by his successful charge, or pleased to help Mary's father? There was more to it. The morning's accidents had helped his stalled imagination picture a kind of employment that offered several attractions. I am not certain that some fibers of Mr. Garth's mind had not begun vibrating again toward the same end that was now becoming clear to Fred. An accident produces results only as a spark does where oil and tinder are ready; and Fred always felt that the railway had supplied the necessary spark. They continued in silence except when the work required them to speak. At last, when they had finished and were walking away, Mr. Garth said:
“A young man doesn't need a B.A. to do work like this, does he, Fred?”
“I wish I'd started it before ever thinking of getting a B.A.,” Fred answered. He hesitated, then added less confidently, “Do you think I'm too old to learn your business, Mr. Garth?”

“My business covers all sorts of things, my boy,” Mr. Garth said with a smile. “Much of what I know only comes with experience. You can't learn it by heart as you do things in a book. But you're still young enough to build a foundation.” Caleb spoke that last sentence firmly, then paused uncertainly. Lately he had understood that Fred had decided to enter the Church.
“You think I could be some use at it, then, if I tried?” Fred asked more eagerly.

“That depends,” Caleb said. He tilted his head and lowered his voice, with the air of someone saying something deeply religious. “You must be certain of two things. First, you must love your work, instead of always looking past it and wishing your free time would begin. Second, you mustn't be ashamed of the work, or think some other occupation would give you more standing. You must take pride in what you do and in learning to do it properly. No forever saying, There's this job and that job—if I had one of those, I could make something of it. Whatever a man does, I wouldn't give twopence for him”—Caleb's mouth tightened bitterly and he snapped his fingers—“whether he's prime minister or thatches haystacks, if he doesn't do well what he's undertaken.”
“I can never feel I'd do that as a clergyman,” Fred said, intending to advance his argument.
“Then don't become one, my boy,” Caleb answered abruptly. “Otherwise you'll never be comfortable with yourself. Or if you _are_ comfortable, you'll be a poor sort of man.”

“That's almost exactly Mary's view,” said Fred, blushing. “I think you must know how I feel about her, Mr. Garth. I hope it doesn't displease you that I've always loved her more than anyone else, and that I'll never love anyone the way I love her.”
As Fred spoke, Caleb's expression visibly softened. But he moved his head with solemn slowness and said:
“That makes it a more serious matter, Fred, if you want Mary's happiness entrusted to you.”

“I know it does, Mr. Garth,” Fred said eagerly, “and I'd do anything for _her_. She says she'll never marry me if I enter the Church. I'll be the most miserable devil alive if I lose all hope of Mary. Truly, if I could find another profession, some business—anything I'm remotely suited to—I'd work hard. I'd earn your respect. I'd like work that involved being outdoors. I already know quite a lot about land and cattle. I used to believe—you'll think it foolish, I know—that I'd have land of my own. I'm sure I could learn that sort of thing easily, especially if I could work under you in some way.”
“Steady, my boy,” said Caleb, seeing “Susan” in his mind's eye. “What have you told your father about this?”

“Nothing yet, but I must tell him. I'm only waiting to find out what I can do instead of going into the Church. I'm very sorry to disappoint him, but surely a man of twenty-four ought to be allowed to decide for himself. How could I have known at fifteen what would be right for me now? My education was a mistake.”
“But listen, Fred,” Caleb said. “Are you certain Mary loves you, or would ever marry you?”

“I asked Mr. Farebrother to speak to her, because she'd forbidden me to—I didn't know what else to do,” Fred said apologetically. “He says I have every reason to hope, if I can establish myself honorably—I mean, outside the Church. You probably think I've no right to trouble you and press my wishes about Mary on you, Mr. Garth, before I've done anything for myself. Of course I've no claim on you at all. In fact, I already owe you a debt that will never be paid off, even when I can repay the money.”

“Yes, my boy, you do have a claim,” Caleb said with deep feeling. “Young people can always claim help from older ones in making a start. I was young once and had to manage with very little help. I'd have welcomed it, if only for the kindness it showed. But I must think. Come to my office tomorrow at nine. The office, mind you.”

Mr. Garth never took an important step without consulting Susan. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that before he got home he had made up his mind. On a great many subjects about which other men were firm or stubborn, he was the easiest man imaginable to manage. He never knew which meat he preferred. If Susan had said they ought to move into a four-room cottage to save money, he would have answered, “Let's go,” without asking for details. But where Caleb's feelings and judgment spoke strongly, he ruled. Despite his gentleness and his reluctance to rebuke anyone, everyone around him knew that on the rare occasions when he chose to insist, he was absolute. Indeed, he only ever chose to insist on someone else's behalf. Mrs. Garth settled ninety-nine points; on the hundredth, she often discovered she must perform the exceptionally difficult task of practicing her own principle and accepting a subordinate place.

“It's turned out as I thought, Susan,” Caleb said when they sat alone that evening. He had described the incident that led Fred to help with his work, but had not yet told her what followed. “The children _are_ fond of each other—I mean Fred and Mary.”
Mrs. Garth lowered her sewing to her lap and fixed her sharp eyes anxiously on her husband.

“After we finished, Fred told me everything. He can't bear the idea of being a clergyman, and Mary says she won't marry him if he becomes one. The boy wants to work under me and turn his mind to business. I've decided to take him on and make a man of him.”
“Caleb!” Mrs. Garth said in a deep contralto that expressed astonishment and resignation together.

“It's a fine thing to do,” Mr. Garth said, settling firmly against the back of his chair and gripping its arms. “He'll give me trouble, but I think I can see it through. The boy loves Mary, and real love for a good woman is a great thing, Susan. It gives shape to many a rough fellow.”
“Has Mary said anything to you about it?” Mrs. Garth asked, secretly a little hurt that she herself had to be told.

“Not a word. I asked about Fred once and gave her a little warning. She assured me she'd never marry an idle, self-indulgent man. Nothing since. But apparently Fred got Mr. Farebrother to speak to her, since she'd forbidden him to speak for himself. Mr. Farebrother discovered that she is fond of Fred, but says he mustn't enter the Church. I can see that Fred's heart is set on Mary. It makes me think well of the boy—and we've always liked him, Susan.”
“I think it's a pity for Mary,” Mrs. Garth said.
“A pity? Why?”
“Because she could have had a man worth twenty Fred Vincys, Caleb.”
“Really?” said Caleb, surprised.

“I'm firmly convinced Mr. Farebrother loves her and intended to propose. Naturally, now that Fred has made him his messenger, that better prospect is finished.” Mrs. Garth spoke with severe precision. She was irritated and disappointed, but determined to waste no words.
Conflicting feelings kept Caleb silent for a few moments. He looked at the floor, moving his head and hands in accompaniment to an inward argument. Finally he spoke:

“That would have made me very proud and happy, Susan. I'd have been glad for your sake. I've always felt that the people belonging to you weren't your equals. Yet you chose me, though I was a plain man.”
“I chose the best and cleverest man I'd ever known,” said Mrs. Garth, quite certain that _she_ could never have loved anyone who fell below that standard.

“Well, perhaps others thought you could have done better. But it would have been worse for me. That's what touches me so closely about Fred. At heart he's good, and he's clever enough to do well if he's set on the right path. He loves and respects my daughter above everything, and she's given him a sort of promise, depending on how he turns out. That young man's soul is in my hands, I tell you. I'll do the best I can for him, so help me God! It's my duty, Susan.”

Mrs. Garth seldom cried, but before her husband finished speaking, a large tear was rolling down her cheek. It came from several feelings pressing together, much affection among them and some irritation. She quickly wiped it away and said:
“Not many men besides you would think it their duty to add to their worries like that, Caleb.”
“What other men think doesn't matter. I have a clear feeling inside me, and I'll follow it. I hope your heart will be with mine, Susan, in making everything as easy as possible for Mary, poor child.”
Leaning back, Caleb looked toward his wife with an anxious appeal. She stood and kissed him. “God bless you, Caleb! Our children have a good father.”

But she went out and cried thoroughly to make up for everything she had left unsaid. She was certain people would misunderstand her husband's actions. Her own judgment of Fred was rational and offered little hope. Which would prove more farsighted: her rationality or Caleb's passionate generosity?
When Fred arrived at the office next morning, he faced a test he had not anticipated.

“Now, Fred,” Caleb said, “there'll be desk work for you. I've always done plenty of writing myself, but I need help. I want you to understand the accounts and get the property values into your head, so I intend to manage without another clerk. You'll have to apply yourself. How are your handwriting and arithmetic?”

Fred's heart gave an uncomfortable jump. Desk work had never occurred to him. But he was feeling determined and would not back away. “Arithmetic doesn't worry me, Mr. Garth. I've always found it easy. I think you've seen my handwriting.”

“Let's have a look,” said Caleb. He picked up a pen, inspected it carefully, dipped it thoroughly, and handed it to Fred with a sheet of ruled paper. “Copy a line or two of that valuation, including the figures at the end.”

At that time people believed it beneath a gentleman to write legibly, or in any hand remotely fit for a clerk. Fred copied the lines in handwriting as gentlemanly as any contemporary viscount's or bishop's. All the vowels looked alike; the consonants could only be told apart by whether they pointed upward or downward. The strokes were solid with inkblots, and the letters scorned to follow the ruled lines. In short, it was the venerable sort of manuscript easily understood if you already know what its writer means.

As Caleb watched, his face grew increasingly downcast. When Fred handed him the sheet, he gave something like a growl and struck it angrily with the back of his hand. Work this bad drove away all Caleb's gentleness.

“Damn it!” he growled. “To think we live in a country where a man's education can cost hundreds upon hundreds of pounds and produce this!” Then, more sorrowfully, he pushed up his spectacles and looked at the unfortunate writer. “Lord have mercy, Fred, I can't accept this!”
“What can I do, Mr. Garth?” Fred asked. He was deeply discouraged, not only by the verdict on his handwriting but by the prospect of being classed with office clerks.

“Do? Learn to shape your letters and stay on the line. What use is writing if no one can read it?” Caleb asked forcefully, entirely absorbed by the poor workmanship. “Is there so little work to do in the world that you need to send puzzles all over the country? But that's how people are brought up. I'd waste endless time on some people's letters if Susan didn't decipher them for me. It's disgraceful.” He flung the paper aside.

A stranger looking into the office just then might have wondered what drama was unfolding between the indignant businessman and the handsome young fellow whose fair complexion was turning blotchy as he bit his lip in humiliation. Many thoughts struggled inside Fred. Mr. Garth had been so kind and encouraging when they first met that morning that gratitude and hope had risen high; now his spirits fell just as far. He had never considered desk work. In fact, like most young gentlemen, he wanted an occupation with nothing unpleasant about it. I cannot say what might have happened if he had not firmly promised himself that he would visit Mary at Lowick and tell her he had been engaged to work under her father. He did not want to lose that pleasure.
“I'm very sorry” was all he could manage to say. But Mr. Garth was already softening.

“We'll have to make the best of it, Fred,” he began in his usual quiet voice. “Anyone can learn to write. I taught myself. Set to it with determination, and stay up at night if you haven't enough time in the day. We'll be patient, my boy. Callum can keep doing the books while you're learning. But I must be off now,” Caleb said, getting up. “Tell your father what we've agreed. Once you can write, you'll save me Callum's salary, you see. I can afford to pay you eighty pounds for the first year, and more afterward.”

When Fred gave his parents the necessary news, the difference in their reactions surprised him and left a deep impression on his memory. He went directly from Mr. Garth's office to the warehouse. He rightly felt that he could show his father most respect by making this painful announcement as seriously and formally as possible. His decision would also be more clearly understood as final if he presented it during his father's most serious hours, which were always those spent in his private room at the warehouse.

Fred came straight to the point. He briefly explained what he had done and what he intended to do, ending by expressing his sorrow at disappointing his father and blaming his own shortcomings. That sorrow was real, and gave him strong, simple words.

Mr. Vincy listened in profound surprise without even an exclamation. In someone so impatient, this silence signaled unusual emotion. Business had already left him in low spirits that morning. As he listened, the slight bitterness around his mouth grew intense. After Fred finished, nearly a minute passed. Mr. Vincy put a book back in his desk and turned the key decisively. Then he looked steadily at his son and said:
“So you've finally decided, have you, sir?”
“I have, father.”
“Very well. Keep to your decision. I've nothing more to say. You've wasted your education and moved down in the world when I gave you the means to rise. That's all.”
“I'm very sorry we disagree, father. I believe I can be as much a gentleman in this work as I could have been as a curate. But I'm grateful that you wanted the best for me.”
“Very well. There's nothing more to say. I wash my hands of you. I only hope that when you have a son, he repays the trouble you take over him better than this.”

This hurt Fred deeply. His father was using the unfair advantage available to us all when we find ourselves in a pitiable position and view our past as though it too were simply part of what deserves sympathy. In truth, Mr. Vincy's ambitions for his son had contained considerable pride, thoughtlessness, and selfish folly. Nevertheless, the disappointed father possessed powerful leverage. Fred felt as if he were being sent away under a curse.
“I hope you won't object to my staying at home, sir?” he said, getting up to leave. “My salary will be enough to pay for my board, which of course I'd wish to do.”

“Board be damned!” said Mr. Vincy, recovering himself in disgust at the suggestion that feeding Fred would make a noticeable difference at his table. “Your mother will want you to stay, naturally. But I won't keep a horse for you, understand, and you'll pay your own tailor. I expect you'll manage with a suit or two less when you're buying them yourself.”
Fred stayed a moment. There was something else he needed to say. At last it came out.
“I hope you'll shake my hand, father, and forgive me for the distress I've caused you.”
Still seated, Mr. Vincy glanced quickly up at his son, who had moved closer. He held out his hand and said hurriedly, “Yes, yes. Let's say no more about it.”

With his mother Fred went through a much fuller account and explanation. But she could not be consoled. She saw something her husband perhaps had never considered: the certainty that Fred would marry Mary Garth. From then on, her own life would be spoiled by an endless influx of Garths and their habits. Her darling boy, with his beautiful face and stylish manner “beyond any other son in Middlemarch,” would surely grow like them in plainness and indifference to clothes. To her, the Garths seemed to have conspired to capture the desirable Fred. She dared not develop that view, however, because even a slight suggestion of it had made him “fly out” at her as never before. She was too sweet-tempered to show anger, but felt her happiness had been bruised. For several days, simply looking at Fred brought a few tears, as if some dreadful prophecy hung over him. Perhaps she recovered her usual cheerfulness more slowly because Fred had warned her not to reopen the painful subject with his father, who had accepted his choice and forgiven him. Had her husband attacked Fred vehemently, she would have been stirred to defend her darling. It was not until the end of the fourth day that Mr. Vincy said:
“Come now, Lucy, my dear, don't be so miserable. You've always spoiled the boy. You'll just have to keep on spoiling him.”
“Nothing's ever hurt me this much, Vincy,” his wife said, her fair throat and chin starting to tremble again, “except when he was ill.”
“Oh, come, never mind! We have to expect trouble with our children. Don't make it worse by letting me see you so unhappy.”
“Well, I won't,” said Mrs. Vincy. The appeal roused her, and she gave herself a small settling shake, like a bird smoothing its ruffled feathers.
“We can't start making such a fuss over one of them,” said Mr. Vincy, wanting to combine a little grumbling with domestic cheerfulness. “There's Rosamond as well as Fred.”
“Yes, poor thing. I was so sorry she lost her baby. But she's recovered nicely.”

“Baby, indeed! I can see Lydgate's making a mess of his practice, and from what I hear he's getting into debt as well. One of these days Rosamond will come to me with a fine story. But they'll get no money from me, I can tell you. Let _his_ family help. I never liked that marriage. Still, talking's no use. Ring for lemons, and stop looking miserable, Lucy. I'll drive you and Louisa to Riverston tomorrow.”
